text: My name is Pajonga, no one in the history books.
But I know everything about Sultan Hasanuddin. He rode me, my body is made of concrete, and I’ve stood tall since 1990 in the yard of Fort Rotterdam, Makassar.

I was made by an artist from France. I don’t know his name. He’s just as unknown as I am. But they say he wanted to present a brave leader through art. Still, without me, Sultan Hasanuddin would have no direction.
I don’t know why my master—Sultan Hasanuddin—raised his hand and pointed somewhere. Since I’ve been standing here, no one has ever explained where he’s pointing.

yesAction.text: Do you want to know what my Master was pointing at?

text: People often argue about the direction of this statue.
This horse statue—does it symbolize resistance, the future, or just the leader’s style in action? I myself have many questions—why am I here? Why are my Master’s statues always shown riding me?
Often, people forget to tell my story. Yet, without me, my Master might never have conquered mountains, crossed rivers, or led battles.
Maybe that’s why the sculptor portrayed us together—because our bond was special. Not everyone can ride a horse, and not every horse can be led into battle.
Do you want to know why horses were important in the nation’s history?

otherAction.text: Do you want to ask something else?

media.description: I’m not very good at reading—you’d better check this yourself.

text: Take your time, read and watch slowly, I’ll give you space.
Ironically, my role is often forgotten.

Yet, I stand at a strategic point, where people can remember history and feel proud. Funny enough, every era paints me in different colors—sometimes green, blue, red—who knows why. But clearly, I’m not just a garden decoration.
Though yes, sometimes we’re just treated as decor.

My friends are the same—standing tall in gardens, in front of grand buildings. Always the same pattern: a park, an important building, and in the middle, a statue of a horse and its rider. As if our histories are connected, crossing countries and time. Perhaps the artist who made me was inspired by European hero statues, then combined it with my Master’s figure.

But the funny thing is, some of my horse friends carry riders who were once my Master’s enemies. I remember clearly—we once went to war against those people, their skin and hair pale, as if untouched by the sun.

But in that war, I also met their horses. We got to know each other, before finally being forced to charge against one another. Ironic, isn’t it? Horses, yet dragged into a war that wasn’t ours. I could show you photos of them from other countries—my friend sent them to me through telepathy.
Do you want to see statues of my friends and their riders? Shall I show you the images?

text: Finish this first, we still have plenty of time.

I want you to know them too. Who knows, maybe our stories are connected. But I still wonder—why weren’t we placed in a forest, where horses truly belong? Even though I am stone now, my form is still a horse.
Actually… I hate gardens. Horses don’t live in gardens. But I am a statue. And I am a horse. I’m confused! Maybe, in the end, my Master and I are just part of Makassar’s city landscaping project?

text: I hope you still like me this far.
But more than that—look closely—our pose is not just random style. Statues of horses like us are symbolic, not just made to look cool on Instagram.

Have you ever imagined how hard it is to sculpt a horse? It can’t be made without meaning. Every detail has a purpose, because we are not just statues, we are part of our Master. We are one story, one trace of history.
Do you want to know the meaning of a horse statue’s pose?

otherAction.text: How can you remember the past?

media.description: Listen! I once heard this as a podcast.

text: No need to rush, please sit down first.
Here, everyone who comes can see the greatness of Sultan Hasanuddin.
I see children running, elders telling stories, and tourists taking pictures. They look at us and remember the past. But if you pass me by—the horse statue—what do you think of?

Or sometimes, just as a place to sit. Because I’m made of concrete. I never move. My legs are fixed on this blue and white base. But in my silence, I keep dreaming. I endure, because of the whisperer—my faithful companion. Do you want me to introduce you to them? Do you want me to take you to the whisperer’s place?

Tell me when you arrive, I’ll tell you my dream about the whisperer.
Have you reached Bastion Buton? Do you see the green building in the middle of the yard?

text: If you’ve reached Bastion Buton, look toward the yard.
There’s a small green building near the coconut tree. Do you know what it was for? Who lived there?
Long ago, the whisperer lived there. I forget her name… Tenriabeng, maybe? Horses really do have short memories.
She was a woman with divine blood—the one who has been singing in your ears along the way. Dreams… oh Tenri. Her voice was soft, like the wind slipping through the old walls of this fort.
I met her back when we were still alive, when I wasn’t a statue, when the fort walls still trembled with soldiers’ footsteps. She was unlike anyone else.
I remember—she never pulled my reins, never gave orders with a harsh voice. She only stood before me, breathed gently, and touched my neck with a hand as light as sea breeze.

She wasn’t a soldier, but she understood my language. She knew when I was scared, when I was tired, when I longed for the pasture. Sometimes she sat beside me and sang quietly—like old verses understood only by stones and animals.
People called her strange, but I knew: she was the whisperer. In Makassar, people like her were rare, but they existed—those who believed horses had sumanga’, had spirit.

I still remember her calm eyes. She didn’t speak much to humans, but she spoke to me. In a language not of words, but of movement and breath. She knew I disliked a tight saddle, knew I wanted to touch water, knew I wasn’t just a war tool, but a loyal friend. Do you feel it now?

It’s said, people like her once chanted spells before troops went to war. They believed horses weren’t just bodies, but souls. If the horse was angry or sad, the battle could be lost. But if the horse trusted, its master would survive.
I don’t know where the whisperer is now. But every night, in my dreams, I still hear her voice. She never ordered me to run.
She only whispered, “Calm, Pajonga. You are not alone.” She whispered too to horses on the streets, straining under heavy loads in the heat, forced to move like machines. Like me now, only stone.
Not far from her house here, the Whisperer also liked to visit the house across. She enjoyed talking with one of the children there—I forgot the name. She said she liked to wander inside the house.
But you know, horse whisperers have always existed. Do you want me to tell you more about her?
Listen calmly, nothing will disturb you.

The horse whisperer often appears in my dreams…

Sometimes, at night, when human voices fade, I—Pajonga—fall asleep in my silence. But this concrete body still dreams. And in my dreams, I am no statue. I live again, in the fort’s yard that was once my home—before I became a symbol, before I became garden decor.
The people of Makassar once saw horses not just as transportation or war vehicles. Horses were friends, symbols of strength and pride.
They respected our steps, the sound of our hooves echoing on the dirt roads and stone corridors of the fort.
In my dream, I remember the past.

In the 1970s, this fort wasn’t a tourist site yet. In one corner of the bastion, I often saw a little child, from a military family living inside the fort. He liked to sneak to me when no one was looking, touch my body, sometimes speak, as if I could answer.
He loved horses dearly, perhaps because of his disciplined upbringing. He wasn’t a soldier, but in his imagination, riding me took him further than any battlefield.
I forgot his name. But one day, I heard: he grew up and became the director of this fort. Maybe he still remembers me.

Or maybe he only sees me now as a monument, not a horse. But I still remember him. I know what it feels like to be trained to obey, but to long for freedom. Or maybe, both of us just wanted to know—like everyone else—where exactly my Master’s hand is pointing?
Do you still remember I La Galigo? What do you recall from the story?
That museum inside—what’s its connection to the fort? Do you know?
As far as I know, I once accompanied my Master against the Bugis. So why did the museum suddenly appear inside the fort?

Truly, I wonder why I’m in a garden, why the bastion home disappeared, why the fort turned into a museum, why what once wasn’t Bugis is now Bugis. So what is history? Am I remembering wrong? What do you think history is?
Do you think horses are part of history? Animals, plants, and objects around you—if they could speak, what would they remember? I will tell you about Makassar’s traditional memory of me.
After this, I will call the whisperer to meet you. Be ready!

yesAction.text: I want to meet the whisperer
